title: Kindness to those who don't fight you
hookLine: Allah doesn't forbid kindness and justice toward those who haven't fought you (60:8)
tomorrow: Why say what you don't do?

lines: CAN SHE BE KIND ACROSS THE LINE?
cards: Asma', the daughter of Abu Bakr, is living in Medina when her mother arrives from Mecca. The mother hasn't become Muslim. Mecca is the city that drove the daughter's community out.
One report says the mother came bearing gifts. Asma' doesn't know what to do. Should she let her in?
Accept the gifts? Can she be kind to her own mother across this line? She goes to ask the Prophet ﷺ.

teach.b: Bukhari and Muslim record his answer. Yes, he said: keep good ties with your mother. Some reports connect this verse to her story.

Pickthall: "Allah forbiddeth you not those who warred not against you on account of religion and drove you not out from your homes, that ye should show them kindness and deal justly with them. Lo! Allah loveth the just dealers."
The first is tabarruhum, show them kindness, from the root b-r-r, the same root as birr, the word the Qur'an and hadith use for kindness to parents.
The second is tuqsitu, deal justly, from qist, fairness.

teach.h: GOD LOVES THE PEOPLE OF FAIRNESS.
teach.b: And the verse ends with God's love for the muqsitin, the people of fairness. So this isn't permission for a cold politeness. It uses family words.
People of another faith who live in peace with the community may be shown birr and qist: warmth and fairness.
The surah came in a hard time, when the community was in conflict with Mecca, and the next verse draws a line around those who actually fought them and drove them out.

Scholars have discussed how the two verses fit together across history. But the core of verse eight is plain: kindness and fairness are not forbidden, and fairness is loved. A mother at the door, not a Muslim.
The answer: yes, be good to her.

how: Muslim scholars cite 60:8 in teaching good relations with neighbors of other faiths, and the story of Asma' bint Abi Bakr and her mother is often told to show that family ties continue across differences of belief.

o: warm kindness, the kind owed to parents
a polite tolerance kept at arm's length
a legal ruling on dealing with enemies

games.q: kindness and justice — tap the pairs.
p: the people of fairness, loved by God

s: the Prophet told Asma' to keep good ties with her mother, who was not Muslim
the verse only allows cold politeness toward people of other faiths
it uses birr, the warm kindness owed to parents, and justice.
the word for kindness in the verse shares a root with kindness to parents
tabarruhum comes from b-r-r, the root of birr.

games.q: you're Asma'. your mother, not a Muslim, has come from Mecca with gifts. what does the Prophet tell you?
o: keep good ties with your mother.
accept the gifts but don't let her in.
games.why: he said yes, keep good ties with your mother, and some reports link verse eight to her story.

practice: Think of someone whose faith, or lack of one, is different from yours: a neighbor, a coworker, a relative, a friend. Picture their face, and breathe in warmth toward them, breathe out fairness.
Then choose one small, concrete kindness, a message, a favor, a genuine question about their week, and hold it until it feels doable.

wordCard.voice: Birr: kindness, the root behind God's permission in Surah Al-Mumtahanah to be warm and fair with those who haven't fought you over faith. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: that you show them kindness and deal justly with them. birr and qist.

carryVoice: Your line: kindness and justice to all. The week ran from deeds sent ahead, through the humbled mountain and the beautiful names, to Ibrahim and Asma' at her door. A full week, done.

sources.q: Allah forbiddeth you not those who warred not against you on account of religion and drove you not out from your homes, that ye should show them kindness and deal justly with them. Lo! Allah loveth the just dealers.

sources.ref: Qur'an 60:9 (those who fought and drove you out)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2620; Sahih Muslim 1003 (Asma' and her mother)
